questions.prompt: Complete with the right form of "to break out": "Nobody could explain the ___ of food poisoning at the summer camp last July."
questions.explanation: After the article "the" the sentence needs a noun, and the noun made from the phrasal verb break out is the compound "outbreak", in which the particle jumps in front of the verb — as in outcome and outlook. The -ing form, the base form and the past form are all verb forms, and none of them gives the ordinary noun this sentence needs.

questions.prompt: Complete: "The Ministry ___ the new timetable at the start of last term."
questions.explanation: "At the start of last term" names a moment that is over and closed, and a closed moment takes the past simple. The present perfect refuses a finished time marker, the present simple would turn the event into a habit, and the past perfect would need a second, later past event to look back from.

questions.prompt: Match each prefix with the base word it combines with to form a real English word.
questions.explanation: The negative prefix chooses its form from the first letter of the word: "im-" before m, p and b gives impatient, and "il-" before l gives illiteracy. "Un-" and "dis-" obey no letter rule and are learnt word by word: unreachable and disability. The tempting mistakes are "unpatient" and "unliteracy", which pick the prefix by ear instead of by spelling. Note that ability also gives inability, a real word with a different meaning — but in- is not on the board here.

questions.prompt: Join these two ideas into ONE sentence that keeps the contrast: "The bus was an hour late." + "Not one pupil missed the examination."

options.text: Although the bus was an hour late, not one pupil missed the examination.
The bus was an hour late, however not one pupil missed the examination.
Although the bus was an hour late, but not one pupil missed the examination.
The bus was an hour late, therefore not one pupil missed the examination.

questions.explanation: "Although" opens a subordinate clause of contrast and the main clause follows after the comma, which joins the two ideas in one sentence. Adding "but" after that clause marks the contrast twice, and one of the two has to go. "However" cannot be glued on with a comma: it needs a full stop or a semicolon before it and a comma right after it. And "therefore" would announce a consequence, the opposite of the contrast the two ideas express.

questions.prompt: Complete: "He has been the head of that primary school ___ 2004."
questions.explanation: "Since" introduces the point in time when the situation started; "for" would introduce its length, as in for twenty-one years; "during" needs a period seen as a whole, as in during the holidays; and "from" opens a stretch that has to be closed by to, as in from 2004 to 2011.

questions.prompt: The word "depression" changes lexical field with the sentence around it. In which of these sentences does it belong to Nature?

options.text: Her doctor treated her for depression for two years.
A deep depression is moving in from the Atlantic.
The depression of the 1930s left millions of workers without a job.
He came back from the holiday in a state of complete depression.

questions.explanation: On a weather map a depression is an area of low pressure, and that is the reading the Atlantic and the movement force here: the word belongs to Nature, next to sandstorm and typhoon. In the doctor's sentence and after the holiday it names a state of mind, and in the 1930s it names a period of economic crisis. One word, three fields — and only the sentence around it decides which one applies.
